sentences.text: Isla's history teacher liked the project very much and had one objection, which was reasonable, and which Isla had already thought of on the bus home.
Drifting.
Whiteout.
A hollow under a ridge fills, the geography changes shape, and a party on foot in a hundred-year storm walks past the mouth of a glen they think they know.
It happens.
It has happened many times, it is in mountain rescue literature, and there is nothing whatever mysterious about it.
The aircraft was harder but not impossible.
Low cloud on the seventh, said the teacher.
Wrong glen.
Smoke does not rise in that kind of cold; it lies down in the hollow and looks like more snow.
Isla wrote all of that in the project, fairly, in its own section, because her great-grandmother had told her to.
That was the thing that surprised her most about the whole business.
She had expected the old woman to defend it.
Instead, when Isla brought the objections back and put them on the table like an accusation, her great-grandmother listened to all of them and said: "Aye.
That'll be it, likely." Isla had come in ready for an argument and had a page of notes, and found herself entirely without a use for either.
"You don't believe that." "I didn't say I believed it.
I said it'll be it." She was doing something with her hands that she had done for eighty years.

"There's a difference between what happened and what you can say happened, and you're eleven, and it's about time you learnt which one goes in a school project." Then she said the other thing, which is the reason Isla has never stopped thinking about any of it.
She said that on the fifth of February 1953, at first light, she had gone out to the peat stack, and there had been a ptarmigan sitting in the scoop on the top of the ridge directly above the hollow.
That it had been there on the sixth.

That it had been there on the seventh, and that her father had seen it too, and that her father — who was not a fanciful man, who kept accounts, who had no patience with any of this — had stood in the yard looking up at the ridge with a bucket in his hand for a long time and had then come in and said nothing at all.
And that on the morning of the eighth it was gone, and by eleven o'clock the party from Ardmore came over the top and down into the hollow without any difficulty whatsoever.
Isla asked the obvious question, which was whether her great-grandmother thought the bird had done it.
The answer took a while.

"I think there was a bird on that ridge for three days and I think on the fourth day there wasn't, and I think thirteen men walked into this glen on the fourth day who couldn't find it on the second." She looked at Isla.
"That's what I know.
Everything past that is what I'd be making up, and I'm ninety-four, and I've watched a lot of people make things up about that week, and I've never once done it and I'm not starting now."
